approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would prevent exporters from lowering anti-dumping duties by temporarily reducing exports.
It would let the minister use alternative methods to calculate an export price when exporters have exported nothing or very little during a review period.
The new methods apply to all reviews lodged or started before the bill starts, but not reviews already finished.
Prescribe a range of methods in new subsection 269TAB(2B) to determine appropriate export prices.
Allow the minister to apply one of these methods to any review not yet finalised.
Require procedural fairness, including notifying affected parties and inviting submissions before a decision.
Exporters subject to anti-dumping and countervailing duties, and Australian industries that may suffer material injury from dumping.

The government introduced the Customs Amendment (Anti-Dumping Measures) Bill 2017 to close a loophole where foreign exporters could limit exports during duty reviews to obtain lower rates and resume dumping. The bill gives the Anti-Dumping Commission three specific methods to set export prices when exporters have made no or unrepresentative exports during a review period, protecting Australian manufacturers and jobs.

The bill closes a loophole that allowed foreign exporters to avoid anti-dumping duties by temporarily reducing exports, then resuming injurious dumping. Labor supported the legislation, citing local manufacturers Capral Aluminium and G.James Glass & Aluminium as examples of businesses affected by dumping.
